claims.text: The dynamic mechanical behavior of high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the formation and interaction of dislocations and stacking faults.
Local elemental distribution and lattice distortion influence dislocation and stacking-fault behavior.
The initial material is a polycrystalline high-entropy alloy containing defects and spatially varying elemental distributions.
The proposed test varies strain rate from 10^-3 to 10^-1 s^-1.
The proposed test varies temperature from room temperature to 800°C.
Energy-filtered 4D-STEM will be used during in situ nanomechanical testing to observe deformation mechanisms.
Dislocation density is a structural mediator of the dynamic mechanical response.
Stacking-fault energy is a structural mediator of the dynamic mechanical response.
Dislocation glide and cross-slip constitute the proposed deformation mechanism.
Local elemental distribution and lattice distortion influence dislocation glide and cross-slip.
Under matched testing conditions, the high-entropy alloy will have 20% greater yield strength than a conventional-alloy baseline such as 316L stainless steel.
Under matched testing conditions, the high-entropy alloy will have 30% greater ductility than a conventional-alloy baseline such as 316L stainless steel.
The hypothesis is proposed to hold between strain rates of 10^-3 and 10^-1 s^-1 and temperatures from room temperature to 800°C.
The exact relationship among local elemental distribution, lattice distortion, and dislocation behavior is not well understood.
The contribution of vacancies and grain boundaries to dynamic mechanical behavior is unclear.
The hypothesis is falsified if yield strength and ductility do not exceed the baseline values by at least 10% under the specified conditions.
